name: Shopify Polaris
tagline: Shopify's admin design system, now shipped as framework-agnostic web components
description: Polaris is the design system every Shopify app and admin surface is built from. As of the 2025 'Polaris unified' release it is a set of 59 custom elements (s-button, s-page, s-money-field, ...) loaded from Shopify's CDN, replacing the deprecated @shopify/polaris React package, which is now archived. It is for developers building Shopify App Home, Admin UI extensions, Checkout UI extensions, Customer accounts and POS surfaces — not a general-purpose library you would drop into an unrelated product.
agent_guidance: Reach for this ONLY inside the Shopify ecosystem — if the task is a Shopify app, embedded admin block or checkout extension, Polaris is mandatory, and anything else in this index (shadcn, MUI, daisyUI) will be rejected by Shopify's review. Critical gotcha: polaris.shopify.com now 301s to shopify.dev/docs/api/polaris, the React package @shopify/polaris is deprecated and its repo is archived, so any model trained on pre-2025 data will emit dead React imports — write s-* custom elements instead. Styling is closed: you cannot theme these with Tailwind, so pair it with plain layout primitives (s-box, s-stack, s-grid) rather than fighting it.
why_it_matters: It is the single largest captive design system on the web — every Shopify app must use it — and the 2025 React-to-web-components pivot is the kind of breaking change an agent will get wrong from memory.
notable_for: Polaris React deprecated and archived in 2025
CDN script, not a bundled npm runtime

name: Atlassian Design System
tagline: Atlaskit: 59 Apache-2.0 React components behind Jira, Confluence and Bitbucket
description: The public documentation for Atlassian's design system, the one that renders Jira, Confluence, Trello and Bitbucket. It ships 59 documented components plus 13 layout primitives (Box, Inline, Stack, Flex, Grid, XCSS), a design token system, and hard-won libraries like Pragmatic drag and drop. Every piece is published to npm as a separately versioned @atlaskit/* package under Apache-2.0, so it is genuinely usable outside Atlassian, though the visual language is unmistakably Atlassian.
agent_guidance: Use this when you are building an actual Atlassian Forge/Connect app, or when you want to read a mature enterprise system's rationale — its docs on tokens, drag and drop, and the UI Styling Standard are better prose than most libraries ship. It publishes an llms.txt, so point a fetch tool there before scraping pages. Do not adopt @atlaskit/* for a generic product: it is per-component npm packages with tight peer-dependency coupling and a css-in-js runtime, which is far heavier to install and theme than shadcn or MUI, and the Atlassian logo/Object components are trademark-bound.
why_it_matters: One of the few enterprise design systems that is both fully documented in public and Apache-2.0 on npm, which makes it a real reference for how a large system handles tokens, primitives and accessibility.

name: Fluent 2
tagline: Microsoft's design system: 47 web components plus Windows, iOS and Android kits
description: Fluent 2 is Microsoft's design system, the visual language behind Windows, Teams, Office and Outlook. This site is the documentation and discovery portal — it documents 47 web components with usage and anatomy guidance, links out to the platform implementations (Fluent UI React v9, WinUI, iOS, Android), and hosts the Figma UI kits and accessibility plugins. The code lives in microsoft/fluentui, where @fluentui/react-components is MIT-licensed and shipped as a single umbrella package over ~60 scoped component packages.
agent_guidance: Prefer Fluent over MUI or shadcn when the product must look native inside Microsoft 365 — a Teams app, an Office add-in, a Windows companion web app — because matching the host chrome is the whole point. Note the split: fluent2.microsoft.design is design guidance and Figma, the actual API reference is storybooks.fluentui.dev, and both are heavy JS sites, so use the llms.txt on fluent2.microsoft.design before scraping. Watch the versioning trap: v8 (@fluentui/react) and v9 (@fluentui/react-components) are different libraries with different APIs, and models routinely mix them — always install @fluentui/react-components for new work.
why_it_matters: The only major design system that documents web, Windows, iOS and Android in one place, which makes it the reference to read when a product must ship consistently across all four.
notable_for: one system across web, Windows, iOS, Android
Figma UI kits and a11y plugins

name: daisyUI
tagline: 68 pure-CSS Tailwind components as semantic class names, MIT, with 35 built-in themes
description: daisyUI is a Tailwind CSS plugin that collapses long utility strings into semantic class names — btn, card, modal — across 68 components. It ships zero JavaScript and no runtime dependency, so it works in any framework or in plain HTML, and it brings 35 ready-made themes plus a CSS-variable theming system out of the box. It is for people who want Tailwind's flexibility without 200-character class attributes, and it is the most-starred free Tailwind component library at 42k stars.
agent_guidance: Reach for daisyUI over shadcn/ui when the stack is not React — Astro, Rails, Django, Laravel, plain HTML — because it is CSS only and needs no component runtime, and when the user wants theme switching for free rather than hand-rolling CSS variables. Its llms.txt is ~79KB of real markdown, so fetch that once and you have the whole API without scraping. The hard limit: daisyUI styles markup but wires nothing — no focus trap, no ARIA state, no keyboard handling on dropdowns or modals — so for anything interactive pair it with Radix, Headless UI, or the native <dialog> element and add the ARIA yourself.
why_it_matters: The default answer for Tailwind-without-the-class-soup, and the rare component library whose CSS-only design makes it portable to every backend framework in the index.
evidence: https://daisyui.com/components/, https://daisyui.com/docs/install/, https://daisyui.com/docs/intro/, https://daisyui.com/docs/themes/, https://daisyui.com/llms.txt, https://api.github.com/repos/saadeghi/daisyui, https://registry.npmjs.org/daisyui

name: Flowbite
tagline: 56+ MIT Tailwind components with vanilla-JS behaviour, plus a paid 450+ block library
description: Flowbite is an open-source Tailwind CSS component library covering over 56 component types with dark mode built in, and unlike CSS-only alternatives it ships a small vanilla-JS package that drives dropdowns, modals, drawers, datepickers and tooltips. The core library is MIT on npm; Flowbite Pro is a separate one-time purchase adding 450+ marketing and application sections plus fully coded pages and a Figma design system. Official wrappers exist for React, Vue, Svelte and Angular, so the same markup travels across stacks.
pricing_detail: Core library free (MIT). Flowbite Pro is a one-time lifetime purchase; third-party listings put it between roughly $149 (designer) and $299 (developer) — flowbite.com/pro/ returned 404 and the pricing helpdesk article returned 402, so treat the exact figure as unverified.
agent_guidance: Pick Flowbite over daisyUI when the user needs working interactive behaviour — dropdowns, modals, drawers, a datepicker — without adding React, because Flowbite ships the vanilla-JS controllers daisyUI deliberately omits. Remember to both `npm install flowbite` and register the plugin/content path, and to import flowbite.js or nothing interactive will fire; in React/Vue prefer the official flowbite-react / flowbite-vue wrappers over the raw data-attribute API. The free tier is genuinely MIT and complete for components — only the 450+ page sections and coded templates sit behind Flowbite Pro, so do not copy Pro block markup into a project.
why_it_matters: The most practical free option when a non-React stack needs Tailwind components that actually behave, filling the gap between CSS-only daisyUI and React-only shadcn.
notable_for: 450+ Pro sections behind a one-time licence
evidence: https://flowbite.com/docs/getting-started/introduction/, https://api.github.com/repos/themesberg/flowbite, https://registry.npmjs.org/flowbite; https://flowbite.com/pro/ 404, https://flowbite.com/blocks/ returned an empty shell, https://flowbite.crisp.help helpdesk article 402 — pricing taken from third-party listings and flagged as unverified

name: Preline UI
tagline: Free Tailwind library with 640+ examples, 204 blocks and documented plugin wiring
description: Preline UI is an open-source Tailwind CSS component set built on a vanilla-JS plugin, covering roughly 73 component families across layout, forms, overlays, navigation and tables — which Preline markets as 640+ ready-made examples plus 204 free blocks and 5 free templates. Its distinguishing feature is the third-party integration layer: documented wiring for advanced select, datatables, charts, maps, datepickers and rich text editors that most free libraries leave to you. Preline Pro adds 780+ blocks and 21 templates (207 pages) as a one-time purchase.

templates.name: Preline free templates

pricing_detail: Open Source: free. Pro: $249 one-time (single developer). Team: $459 one-time (up to 15 developers). Enterprise: custom. Free tier includes 640+ components, 204 blocks and 5 templates; Pro/Team add 780+ blocks and 21 templates totalling 207 pages. Redistribution is prohibited on free and paid tiers; only Enterprise permits it under separate terms.
agent_guidance: Choose Preline when the build needs the awkward widgets — a searchable advanced select, a datatable, a chart, a map, a rich text editor — because it documents the third-party wiring instead of leaving you to integrate Choices.js or ApexCharts yourself; daisyUI and Flowbite both stop short of that. Read the licence before copying: it is dual MIT + 'Preline UI Fair Use License', and redistribution is explicitly forbidden on both free and paid tiers, so never emit Preline markup into a component library or template you intend to publish. The '640+ components' figure is marketing for example variants — the real surface is about 73 component families, so verify a component exists in the docs before you assume it.
why_it_matters: The free Tailwind library with the widest integration surface, and the one whose licence has a redistribution trap that an agent copy-pasting blocks will otherwise walk straight into.
notable_for: dual MIT + Fair Use licence, no redistribution
